flawed_step: A proof would have to show that the flow decomposes into F unit s-t paths that together use at least F+1 distinct arcs. That means at least one path must have length 2 or more. Nothing forces this: an arc can go straight from s to t. That path has length 1 and uses one arc for one unit of flow. So the step "some path in the decomposition has length at least 2" cannot be justified.
counterexample: Vertices {s, t, u, v}. The only arc is (s,t), with capacity 1; u and v are isolated, which the definitions allow. The only s-t cut value is 1, so the maximum flow value is F = 1 > 0. The only feasible flow of value 1 is f(s,t) = 1, since there are no other arcs, so this is the unique maximum flow. It gives positive flow to exactly 1 arc, but the statement requires at least F+1 = 2. The same thing happens with no isolated vertices: take arcs s->t, s->u, u->v. Here F = 1, and in any maximum flow the arcs s->u and u->v must carry 0, because flow into v cannot leave v. So again only 1 arc carries flow.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. If there is a direct arc from s to t, a maximum flow can use only that arc. With the single arc (s,t) on 4 vertices, F = 1 and the unique maximum flow gives positive flow to exactly 1 arc, which is fewer than F+1 = 2.
